steps.say: We see because light enters our eyes. About 1,000 years ago, Ibn al-Haytham showed this with careful experiments.

figure.alt: Light travels from a light source to an object, then reflects into an eye.

steps.say: Most objects do not make light. We see them because light from a source reflects off them into our eyes.
Smooth, shiny surfaces reflect light in a regular way and make clear images. Rough surfaces scatter light.
When light hits a mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both are measured from the normal.
Light changes direction when it passes from one material into another, such as from water into air. This is refraction.
Refraction makes a straw look bent and a pool look shallower. A prism splits white light into colours, as Newton showed in 1666.

check.prompt: How do we see a red apple?

options.text: Light comes out of our eyes and lands on the apple.
options.why: Our eyes take in light. They do not give it out.

options.text: The apple makes its own red light.
options.why: An apple is not a light source.

options.text: We see it even in total darkness.
options.why: Without any light, we cannot see the apple.

options.text: Light reflects off the apple into our eyes.

hints: An apple is not a light source.
Light must travel from a source, to the apple, to your eye.
Cross out the choices where the light starts at the eye or the apple.
check.explanation: Light from a source hits the apple and reflects into our eyes. That is how we see objects that do not make their own light.

check.prompt: The bending of light as it passes from water into air is called ___.
hints: It makes a straw in water look bent.
It is different from reflection, where light bounces back.
The word starts with the same two letters as reflection, but it means bending.
check.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one material into another.
